claim: CsChrimson expression was observed in specific neuronal clusters that correspond to previously characterized dsx, fru-co-expressing neurons in the male brain and ventral nerve cord, including P1/pC1 neurons.
source: We observed CsChrimson expression in specific neuronal clusters that correspond to previously characterized dsx, fru-co-expressing neurons in the male brain and ventral nerve cord, including P1/pC1 neurons (Figure 1A,B, Figure 1—figure supplement 1A; Rideout et al., 2007; Rideout et al., 2010; Sanders and Arbeitman, 2008; Zhou et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 1A,B and Figure 1—figure supplement 1A, and is corroborated by citations to previous studies.

claim: Very few labeled cells were found in the female brain expressing CsChrimson under dsxGAL4 and fruFLP control.
source: In contrast, we found very few labeled cells in the female brain (Figure 1B, Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 1B and Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claim: The number of cells labeled by the dsxGAL4 ∩ fruFLP approach was significantly fewer than neurons reported to co-express dsx and fru by immunohistochemistry.
source: We note that the number of cells labeled by our approach was significantly fewer than neurons reported to co-express dsx and fru by immunohistochemistry (Rideout et al., 2007) likely because of a mismatch between knock-in alleles and endogenous gene expression patterns (Stockinger et al., 2005; Yu et al., 2010), a difference in the expression levels of UAS transgenic elements (Pfeiffer et al., 2010; Pfeiffer et al., 2012), or an incomplete excision by FLP of the transcriptional termination signals (Nern et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by comparison to previous immunohistochemistry studies and is explained by citing known technical limitations of the genetic approach.

claim: Optogenetic activation of dsxGAL4 ∩ fruFLP neurons induced both wing extensions and lunges toward male target flies.
source: When the target fly was male, optogenetic activation of dsxGAL4 ∩ fruFLP neurons induced both wing extensions and lunges across a range of stimulation LED frequencies (Figure 1E,F, Figure 1—figure supplement 3A; see also Video 1 – part 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 1E,F and Figure 1—figure supplement 3A, and by Video 1.

claim: Optogenetic activation of dsxGAL4 ∩ fruFLP neurons induced robust wing extensions but no lunges toward female target flies.
source: Toward a female target fly, the same optogenetic activation induced robust wing extensions (Figure 1G3–H3, Figure 1—figure supplement 3B3) but no lunges (Figure 1G2, H2, I2, Figure 1—figure supplement 3B2) (see also Video 1 – part 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by behavioral data shown in multiple figure panels and by Video 1.

claim: The presence of female target flies induced more wing extensions from tester flies than did the presence of male target flies.
source: The presence of female target flies induced more wing extensions from tester flies than did the presence of male target flies (Figure 1I3).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative behavioral data shown in Figure 1I3.

claim: Optogenetic activation of dsxGAL4 ∩ fruFLP neurons increased time orienting toward females more than it did toward males.
source: Optogenetic activation of dsxGAL4 ∩ fruFLP neurons also increased time orienting toward females more than it did toward males (Figure 1E1, I1), suggesting that the lack of lunges toward female targets is not due to the lack of opportunities to interact (due to immobility, for instance).
evidence: The claim is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 1E1 and I1, and includes an inference about the reason for the lack of lunges.

claim: Activation of dsxGAL4 ∩ fruFLP neurons by itself does not determine the behavior of the tester fly; behaviors are influenced by target flies.
source: We therefore conclude that activation of dsxGAL4 ∩ fruFLP neurons can induce more wing extensions toward female than toward male targets, and lunges only if a male target fly is present. In other words, the activation of this neuronal population by itself does not determine the behavior of the tester fly. Even under optogenetic manipulations, behaviors of tester flies are influenced by target flies, likely through sex-specific sensory cues or subtle behaviors of target flies that are currently not quantified.
evidence: The claim is a conclusion drawn from the behavioral data presented in the preceding figures and represents an inference about the mechanism.

claim: NP2631 ∩ dsxFLP neurons include a specific subset of P1/pC1 neurons that is reported to promote both courtship and aggression toward a male target.
source: This population includes a specific subset of P1/pC1 neurons that is reported to promote both courtship and aggression toward a male target (Koganezawa et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: Optogenetic activation of NP2631 ∩ dsxFLP neurons robustly increased both wing extensions and lunges toward male target flies.
source: Consistent with this, we found that the optogenetic activation of NP2631 ∩ dsxFLP neurons robustly increased both wing extensions and lunges toward male target flies (Figure 2A, Figure 2—figure supplement 1A; see also Video 2 – part 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 2A and Figure 2—figure supplement 1A, and by Video 2.

claim: Optogenetic activation of NP2631 ∩ dsxFLP neurons did not trigger lunges when the target flies were females.
source: Interestingly, however, the same manipulation did not trigger lunges when the target flies were females (Figure 2B2, Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 2B2 and Figure 2—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Activation of NP2631 ∩ dsxFLP neurons in the presence of female target flies induced more wing extensions during LED stimulations than during ISIs.
source: Instead, activation of NP2631 ∩ dsxFLP neurons in the presence of female target flies induced more wing extensions during LED stimulations than during ISIs (Figure 2B3; see also Video 2 – Part 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 2B3 and by Video 2.

claim: Time orienting toward both male and female targets increased after optogenetic stimulation of NP2631 ∩ dsxFLP neurons.
source: Time orienting toward both male and female targets increased after optogenetic stimulation of NP2631 ∩ dsxFLP neurons (Figure 2A1, B1), excluding the possibility that tester males did not have an opportunity to lunge toward female targets.
evidence: The claim is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 2A1 and B1, and includes an inference about the interpretation.

claim: Optogenetic stimulation of NP2631 ∩ dsxFLP neurons in the absence of target flies did not induce a lunge-like behavior or change in speed.
source: However, in contrast to the previous observation (Koganezawa et al., 2016), we did not observe a lunge-like behavior or change in speed when we optogenetically stimulate NP2631 ∩ dsxFLP neurons in the absence of target flies (Figure 2—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: The claim is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1D and contrasts with a previous study.

claim: The function of NP2631 ∩ dsxFLP neurons depends on the sex of target flies.
source: Thus, the function of NP2631 ∩ dsxFLP neurons depends on the sex of target flies.
evidence: The claim is a conclusion drawn from the behavioral data presented in the preceding figures.

claim: CsChrimson expression was consistently detected in a single pair of neuronal clusters located at the medial posterior region of male brains in NP2631 ∩ dsxFLP flies.
source: With the genetic reagents we used (UAS > stop > CsChrimson:tdTomato as a reporter as well as an effector element: see Supplementary file 1 for details), we consistently detected expression of CsChrimson:tdTomato in a single pair of neuronal clusters located at the medial posterior region of male brains (23 out of 23 brains examined in Figure 2—figure supplement 2D1; orange circles in Figure 2—figure supplement 2A1; see also Video 3).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2A1 and D1, and by Video 3.

claim: Nearly all NP2631 ∩ dsxFLP cell bodies express Dsx proteins, and a subset of them also co-express FruM proteins.
source: As was reported in Koganezawa et al. (2016), we found that nearly all of these cell bodies express Dsx proteins, and a subset of them also co-express FruM proteins (Figure 2—figure supplement 2B,C), indicating that they belong to the 'P1/pC1' neuronal cluster.
evidence: The claim is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2B,C and is corroborated by a citation.

claim: A descending neuron with a large cell body and a tract not shared with the P1/pC1 cluster was occasionally observed in NP2631 ∩ dsxFLP flies.
source: In addition, we occasionally observed a neuron with a large cell body and a tract that is not shared with the P1/pC1 cluster. This neuron has a prominent arborization in the contralateral ventromedial neuropil and a long descending fiber through the entire ventral nerve cord (Figure 2—figure supplement 2A2).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2A2.

claim: The descending neuron was present in up to 35% of male brains, all of which had only one such neuron in one of the two hemispheres.
source: This descending neuron was present in up to 35% of male brains, all of which had only one such neuron in one of the two hemispheres (Figure 2 – figure supplement D1).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2D1.

claim: An increase in both lunges and wing extensions upon optogenetic stimulation of NP2631 ∩ dsxFLP neurons was observed far more consistently than the presence of the descending neuron.
source: Importantly, we observed an increase in both lunges and wing extensions upon optogenetic stimulation of NP2631 ∩ dsxFLP neurons far more consistently than the presence of the descending neuron (Figure 2—figure supplements 2D2 and 3).
evidence: The claim is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2D2 and 3.

claim: The behavioral effects by the activation of NP2631 ∩ dsxFLP neurons are due to its P1/pC1 neuronal cluster.
source: Based on this observation, we conclude that the behavioral effects by the activation of NP2631 ∩ dsxFLP neurons are due to its P1/pC1 neuronal cluster.
evidence: The claim is a conclusion drawn from the data showing the inconsistency between the presence of the descending neuron and behavioral effects.

claim: Suppression of CsChrimson expression in fruP1.LexA-expressing subpopulations significantly reduced the amount of optogenetically induced lunges and wing extensions compared to controls.
source: When the expression of CsChrimson was suppressed in fruP1.LexA-expressing subpopulations, the amount of optogenetically induced lunges and wing extensions were both significantly decreased compared to controls that have CsChrimson in all NP2631 ∩ dsxFLP neurons (Figure 2C).
evidence: The claim is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: The amount of lunges during LED stimulations in flies with CsChrimson suppressed in fruP1.LexA-expressing neurons was still significantly higher than those before LED stimulations or during ISIs.
source: The amount of lunges during LED stimulations in this genotype was still significantly higher than those before LED stimulations or during ISIs (Figure 2C2), which can be due to some fruP1.LexA-negative neurons that specifically promote aggression (Koganezawa et al., 2016), or incomplete suppression of NP2631 in fruP1.LexA-expressing neurons in some animals.
evidence: The claim is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 2C2 and includes speculation about the mechanism.

claim: The significant reduction of lunges and wing extensions in the absence of the fruP1.LexA-expressing subgroup favors the idea that the fru-expressing subpopulation (NP2631 ∩ dsxFLP ∩ fruP1.LexA) is capable of promoting both behaviors.
source: Regardless, the significant reduction of lunges and wing extensions in the absence of the fruP1.LexA-expressing subgroup favors the idea that the fru-expressing subpopulation (NP2631 ∩ dsxFLP ∩ fruP1.LexA) is capable of promoting both behaviors.
evidence: The claim is a conclusion drawn from the behavioral data presented in Figure 2C.

claim: NP2631 ∩ dsxFLP neurons contain dsx and fru-expressing subset of P1/pC1 neurons that can promote courtship and aggressive behaviors depending on the sex of target flies.
source: These results led us to conclude that NP2631 ∩ dsxFLP neurons contain dsx and fru-expressing subset of P1/pC1 neurons that can promote courtship and aggressive behaviors depending on the sex of target flies (Figure 2D).
evidence: The claim is a conclusion drawn from the behavioral and genetic data presented in the preceding sections.

claim: More NP2631 ∩ dsxFLP neurons are labeled in males than in females.
source: We observed that more NP2631 ∩ dsxFLP neurons are labeled in males than in females (Figure 3G).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 3G.

claim: NP2631 ∩ dsxFLP neurons in both sexes extend a single tract that innervates the lateral protocerebral complex including commissural projections at the superior dorsal protocerebrum.
source: NP2631 ∩ dsxFLP neurons in both sexes extend a single tract that innervates the so-called lateral protocerebral complex (Yu et al., 2010) including commissural projections at the superior dorsal protocerebrum (Figure 3C2, F2).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 3C2 and F2, and is corroborated by a citation.

claim: Male NP2631 ∩ dsxFLP neurons have thicker projections at the lateral junctions than female neurons.
source: Firstly, male neurons have thicker projections at the lateral junctions (orange in Figure 3H,K; Figure 3L; Yu et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 3H, K, and L, and is corroborated by a citation.

claim: Male NP2631 ∩ dsxFLP neurons consistently have a lateral segment branching within the 'ring' projection ('lateral vertical projection') that female neurons almost completely lack.
source: Secondly, male neurons consistently have a lateral segment branching within the 'ring' projection (Yu et al., 2010) ('lateral vertical projection') that female neurons almost completely lack (green in Figure 3H,K; Figure 3M).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 3H, K, and M, and is corroborated by a citation.

claim: Female NP2631 ∩ dsxFLP neurons have more extensive projections at the superior medial part of the brain ('superior medial projection') than male neurons.
source: Thirdly, female neurons have more extensive projections at the superior medial part of the brain ('superior medial projection') (magenta in Figure 3H,K; Figure 3N) (see also Video 3).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 3H, K, and N, and by Video 3.

claim: NP2631 ∩ dsxFLP neurons are sexually dimorphic.
source: Thus, NP2631 ∩ dsxFLP neurons are sexually dimorphic.
evidence: The claim is a conclusion drawn from the neuroanatomical data presented in the preceding sections.

claim: In fruF males, NP2631 ∩ dsxFLP neurons are similar to male neurons in cell body number and all three sexually dimorphic neuroanatomical characteristics.
source: Indeed, we found P1a neurons in fruF males (Figure 6C), but not in fruM females (Figure 6B). The number of P1a cell bodies was comparable between males and fruF males (Figure 6E). Interestingly, registered P1a neurons in male and fruF male brains showed quantitative differences in their neuroanatomy.
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 3G, J, L-N and by Video 4.

claim: NP2631 ∩ dsxFLP neurons in fruM females are similar to those of females in cell body number and two of the three sexually dimorphic neuroanatomical characteristics.
source: while NP2631 ∩ dsxFLP neurons in fruM females (Figure 3D) are similar to those of females in cell body number and two of the three characteristics (Figure 3G,I,L–M (blue); see also Video 5).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 3G, I, L-M and by Video 5.

claim: The only exception to the similarity between fruM females and wild-type females was the size of superior medial projection, which in fruM females was comparable to that in males.
source: The only exception was the size of superior medial projection, which in this genotype was comparable to that in males (Figure 3N).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 3N.

claim: Morphological sexual dimorphisms of NP2631 ∩ dsxFLP neurons are established predominantly by the sexual dimorphism of dsx.
source: These observations suggest that morphological sexual dimorphisms of NP2631 ∩ dsxFLP neurons are established predominantly by the sexual dimorphism of dsx.
evidence: The claim is a conclusion drawn from the neuroanatomical data comparing different genotypes.

claim: Complete transformation of NP2631 ∩ dsxFLP neurons to the female type may also require the cooperative contribution of fru.
source: Complete transformation of this class of neurons to the female type may also require the cooperative contribution of fru.
evidence: The claim is a speculation based on the observation that the superior medial projection in fruM females was not fully transformed to the female type.

claim: Presence of the fru4-40 allele by itself did not affect overall sexually dimorphic characteristics of NP2631 ∩ dsxFLP neurons.
source: Presence of the fru4-40 allele by itself did not affect overall sexually dimorphic characteristics of NP2631 ∩ dsxFLP neurons (Figure 3G, Figure 3—figure supplement 1A–H).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 3G and Figure 3—figure supplement 1A-H.

claim: Activation of NP2631 ∩ dsxFLP neurons induced qualitatively similar behavioral changes in males with the fru locus of +/+, +/fru4-40, or fruM/fru4-40.
source: Activation of this population induced qualitatively similar behavioral changes in males with the fru locus of +/+, +/fru4-40, or fruM/fru4-40 (Figure 3—figure supplement 1I).
evidence: The claim is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1I.

claim: Optogenetic activation of NP2631 ∩ dsxFLP neurons in fruF males increased both time orienting and wing extensions toward both males and females.
source: Optogenetic activation of NP2631 ∩ dsxFLP neurons in fruF males increased both time orienting (Figure 4A1, B1) and wing extensions (Figure 4A3, B3), toward both males and females (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A,B; see also Video 6).
evidence: The claim is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 4A1, B1, A3, B3 and Figure 4—figure supplement 1A,B, and by Video 6.

claim: NP2631 ∩ dsxFLP neurons are capable of generating at least an aspect of male-type courtship behavior in a fruM-independent manner.
source: This result suggests that this neuronal population is indeed capable of generating at least an aspect of male-type courtship behavior in a fruM-independent manner.
evidence: The claim is a conclusion drawn from the behavioral data in fruF males.

claim: In fruF males, the amount of wing extensions toward male and female target flies was comparable after optogenetic activation of NP2631 ∩ dsxFLP neurons.
source: Interestingly, in fruF males, the amount of wing extensions toward male and female target flies was comparable after optogenetic activation of NP2631 ∩ dsxFLP neurons (Figure 4C, right).
evidence: The claim is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: In regular males, optogenetic activation of NP2631 ∩ dsxFLP neurons induced more wing extensions toward females than toward males.
source: This is in contrast to the situation in regular males, which performed more wing extensions toward females (Figure 4C, left).
evidence: The claim is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Optogenetic activation of NP2631 ∩ dsxFLP neurons in regular males and in fruF males induced a similar amount of wing extensions toward male targets.
source: Nonetheless, optogenetic activation of NP2631 ∩ dsxFLP neurons in regular males and in fruF males induced a similar amount of wing extensions toward male targets (Figure 4C), suggesting that the lack of fruM specifically abrogates tester flies' capacity to enhance the intensity of courtship behavior selectively toward females.
evidence: The claim is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 4C and includes an inference about the role of fruM.

claim: The lack of fruM specifically abrogates tester flies' capacity to enhance the intensity of courtship behavior selectively toward females.
source: Nonetheless, optogenetic activation of NP2631 ∩ dsxFLP neurons in regular males and in fruF males induced a similar amount of wing extensions toward male targets (Figure 4C), suggesting that the lack of fruM specifically abrogates tester flies' capacity to enhance the intensity of courtship behavior selectively toward females.
evidence: The claim is an inference drawn from the behavioral data comparing regular males and fruF males.

claim: fruF males do not show lunges.
source: fruF males do not show lunges (Lee and Hall, 2000; Vrontou et al., 2006), which suggests that the execution mechanism for male-type aggressive behavior depends on fruM.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies and includes an inference about the mechanism.

claim: Optogenetic activation of NP2631 ∩ dsxFLP neurons in fruF males induced almost no lunges toward either target sex.
source: In fact, the same optogenetic manipulation induced almost no lunges toward either target sex (Figure 4A2, B2; see also Video 6).
evidence: The claim is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 4A2 and B2, and by Video 6.

claim: For courtship, dsx specifies NP2631 ∩ dsxFLP neurons as an execution component, while amplification of this function specifically toward female targets is fruM-dependent.
source: We therefore conclude that sexual dimorphism in dsx and fru genes have different impacts on the function of NP2631 ∩ dsxFLP neurons. For courtship, dsx specifies NP2631 ∩ dsxFLP neurons as an execution component, while amplification of this function specifically toward female targets is fruM-dependent (Figure 4D).
evidence: The claim is a conclusion drawn from the behavioral and genetic data presented in the preceding sections.

claim: A fruM-dependent mechanism is necessary for NP2631 ∩ dsxFLP neurons to promote male-type aggressive behaviors, even though gross neuroanatomy of this population is specified primarily by dsx.
source: On the other hand, a fruM-dependent mechanism is necessary for NP2631 ∩ dsxFLP neurons to promote male-type aggressive behaviors, even though gross neuroanatomy of this population is specified primarily by dsx.
evidence: The claim is a conclusion drawn from the behavioral and neuroanatomical data presented in the preceding sections.

claim: P1a neurons appeared only in male flies.
source: P1a neurons appeared only in male flies (Hoopfer et al., 2015; Figure 6A,D).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 6A and D, and is corroborated by a citation.

claim: The lack of P1a labeling in females likely reflects the absence of P1a neurons, since dsx and fru-co-expressing neurons in the posterior part of the brain are known to undergo DsxF-dependent apoptosis.
source: The lack of labeling in females likely reflects the absence of P1a neurons, since dsx and fru-co-expressing neurons in the posterior part of the brain are known to undergo DsxF-dependent apoptosis (Kimura et al., 2008; Sanders and Arbeitman, 2008).
evidence: The claim is an inference based on known mechanisms of neuronal apoptosis, supported by citations.

claim: P1a neurons were found in fruF males but not in fruM females.
source: Indeed, we found P1a neurons in fruF males (Figure 6C), but not in fruM females (Figure 6B).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 6B and C.

claim: The number of P1a cell bodies was comparable between males and fruF males.
source: The number of P1a cell bodies was comparable between males and fruF males (Figure 6E).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 6E.

claim: Registered P1a neurons in male and fruF male brains showed quantitative differences in their neuroanatomy.
source: Interestingly, registered P1a neurons in male and fruF male brains showed quantitative differences in their neuroanatomy.
evidence: The claim is supported by neuroanatomical data presented in the following sentences and figures.

claim: Innervations of P1a neurons in fruF males were generally thinner than in males.
source: Most notably, innervations of P1a neurons in fruF males were generally thinner.
evidence: The claim is supported by neuroanatomical data presented in the following figures.

claim: The volume of projections at the lateral junction was smaller in fruF males than in males.
source: We specifically found that the volume of projections at the lateral junction was smaller in fruF males than in males (Figure 6F,G,H).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 6F, G, and H.

claim: Neural processes emanating from the posterior side of the lateral junction ('dorsal posterior projection') was more prominent in fruF males than in males.
source: In contrast, neural processes emanating from the posterior side of the lateral junction ('dorsal posterior projection') was more prominent in fruF males than in males (Figure 6F,G,I; see also Video 8).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 6F, G, and I, and by Video 8.

claim: Sexually dimorphic characteristics of the P1a neurons are specified by both dsx and fru.
source: These observations indicate that sexually dimorphic characteristics of the P1a neurons are specified by both dsx and fru.
evidence: The claim is a conclusion drawn from the neuroanatomical data comparing different genotypes.

claim: Cooperative roles of dsx and fru on P1a neurons are reminiscent of the previous report on the roles of the two genes in a fru-expressing P1/pC1 neuronal cluster labeled by different genetic reagents.
source: Such cooperative roles of dsx and fru are reminiscent of the previous report on the roles of the two genes in a fru-expressing P1/pC1 neuronal cluster labeled by different genetic reagents (Kimura et al., 2008).
evidence: The claim is an inference based on comparison to a previous study, supported by a citation.

claim: Presence of the fru4-40 allele did not affect the overall morphology of P1a neurons.
source: Similar to the case in NP2631 ∩ dsxFLP neurons, presence of the fru4-40 allele did not affect the overall morphology of P1a neurons (Figure 6E, Figure 6—figure supplement 1A–F) or the behavioral effect of optogenetic stimulations (Figure 6—figure supplement 1G), although lunges toward males were not as robustly induced in the presence of the fru4-40 allele.
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 6E and Figure 6—figure supplement 1A-F.

claim: Optogenetic activation of P1a neurons in fruF males robustly increased time orienting toward both male and female target flies.
source: Optogenetic activation of P1a neurons in fruF males robustly increased time orienting toward both male and female target flies (Figure 6—figure supplement 2A1, B1), but its capacity to promote wing extensions was severely impaired.
evidence: The claim is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2A1 and B1.

claim: The capacity of P1a neurons in fruF males to promote wing extensions was severely impaired.
source: Optogenetic activation of P1a neurons in fruF males robustly increased time orienting toward both male and female target flies (Figure 6—figure supplement 2A1, B1), but its capacity to promote wing extensions was severely impaired.
evidence: The claim is supported by behavioral data presented in the following sentences and figures.

claim: Sporadic wing extensions during LED stimulations and ISIs in fruF males were significantly more frequent than wing extensions performed by genetic controls.
source: We observed sporadic wing extensions during LED stimulations and ISIs, which were significantly more frequent than wing extensions performed by genetic controls (Figure 6—figure supplement 2A3, B3).
evidence: The claim is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2A3 and B3.

claim: The amount of optogenetically induced wing extensions in fruF males was significantly less than what P1a neurons in normal males induced toward male targets.
source: However, the amount of optogenetically induced wing extensions was significantly less than what P1a neurons in normal males induced toward male targets (Figure 6—figure supplement 2C), which is in contrast to the situation in male NP2631 ∩ dsxFLP neurons.
evidence: The claim is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2C.

claim: Optogenetic activation of P1a neurons in fruF males induced virtually no lunges.
source: Similar to NP2631 ∩ dsxFLP neurons, optogenetic activation of P1a neurons in fruF males induced virtually no lunges (Figure 6—figure supplement 2A2, B2).
evidence: The claim is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2A2 and B2.

claim: NP2631 ∩ dsxFLP and P1a neurons are distinct not only in neuroanatomy and behavioral roles, but also in the genetic specification mechanisms.
source: Overall, these results demonstrate that NP2631 ∩ dsxFLP and P1a neurons are distinct not only in neuroanatomy and behavioral roles, but also in the genetic specification mechanisms.
evidence: The claim is a conclusion drawn from the neuroanatomical, behavioral, and genetic data presented in the preceding sections.

claim: Genetic and functional diversity within the dsx and fru-co-expressing P1/pC1 cluster suggests that Drosophila social behavior can be tuned at a multitude of circuit nodes.
source: Genetic and functional diversity within the dsx and fru-co-expressing P1/pC1 cluster suggests that Drosophila social behavior can be tuned at a multitude of circuit nodes.
evidence: The claim is an inference drawn from the observed diversity within the P1/pC1 cluster.

claim: dsx plays a major role in establishing a neuronal circuit that enables the male flies to execute courtship behavior.
source: These results suggest that dsx plays a major role in establishing a neuronal circuit that enables the male flies to execute courtship behavior, whereas fru is critical for enhancing courtship behavior toward females, likely through proper recognition of target sex.
evidence: The claim is a conclusion drawn from the behavioral and genetic data presented in the study.

claim: fru is critical for enhancing courtship behavior toward females, likely through proper recognition of target sex.
source: These results suggest that dsx plays a major role in establishing a neuronal circuit that enables the male flies to execute courtship behavior, whereas fru is critical for enhancing courtship behavior toward females, likely through proper recognition of target sex.
evidence: The claim is a conclusion drawn from the behavioral and genetic data presented in the study.

claim: The fact that the sex of the target flies influences the function of P1/pC1 subsets implies that information about target sex can modulate the neural circuit units downstream of these neurons.
source: The fact that the sex of the target flies influences the function of P1/pC1 subsets implies that information about target sex can modulate the neural circuit units downstream of these neurons, and encourages us to revise the linear circuit model for sexually dimorphic social behaviors.
evidence: The claim is an inference drawn from the observed influence of target sex on neuronal function.

claim: The complete specification and courtship-promoting functions of P1a neurons require both dsx and fru.
source: In contrast, the complete specification and courtship-promoting functions of P1a neurons require both dsx and fru, revealing genetic and functional heterogeneity within P1/pC1 neurons.
evidence: The claim is a conclusion drawn from the neuroanatomical and behavioral data comparing different genotypes.

claim: NP2631 ∩ dsxFLP and P1a neurons require a fruM-dependent mechanism to promote male-type aggressive behavior.
source: Lastly, NP2631 ∩ dsxFLP and P1a neurons require a fruM-dependent mechanism to promote male-type aggressive behavior.
evidence: The claim is a conclusion drawn from the behavioral data in fruF males.

claim: Neither NP2631 ∩ dsxFLP nor P1a neurons are part of the execution mechanism for male-type aggressive behavior.
source: This suggests that neither of these neurons are part of the execution mechanism for male-type aggressive behavior, and that the genetic mechanisms specifying execution components for courtship and aggressive behaviors are different.
evidence: The claim is an inference drawn from the observation that these neurons require fruM to promote aggression.

claim: The genetic mechanisms specifying execution components for courtship and aggressive behaviors are different.
source: This suggests that neither of these neurons are part of the execution mechanism for male-type aggressive behavior, and that the genetic mechanisms specifying execution components for courtship and aggressive behaviors are different.
evidence: The claim is an inference drawn from the differential roles of dsx and fru in courtship and aggression.

claim: Attacks triggered by optogenetic stimulation of ventrolateral hypothalamus (VMH) in male mice tend to last longer toward castrated males than toward female targets.
source: In fact, attacks triggered by optogenetic stimulation of ventrolateral hypothalamus (VMH) in male mice tend to last longer toward castrated males than toward female targets (Lin et al., 2011), and chemogenetic activation of progesterone receptor-expressing VMH neurons appears to induce more attacks toward male than toward female targets (Yang et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies in mice.

claim: Chemogenetic activation of progesterone receptor-expressing VMH neurons appears to induce more attacks toward male than toward female targets.
source: In fact, attacks triggered by optogenetic stimulation of ventrolateral hypothalamus (VMH) in male mice tend to last longer toward castrated males than toward female targets (Lin et al., 2011), and chemogenetic activation of progesterone receptor-expressing VMH neurons appears to induce more attacks toward male than toward female targets (Yang et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to a previous study in mice.

claim: The target sex has a significant impact on behavioral choice even for optogenetically induced social behaviors.
source: While effects on target sex are not consistently documented, our results and above-mentioned previous observations in mice show that the target sex has a significant impact on behavioral choice even for optogenetically induced social behaviors.
evidence: The claim is a conclusion drawn from the current study's results and previous observations in mice.

claim: Sensory or behavioral feedback from target animals can impact the operation of what may appear to be an 'execution mechanism' for a given behavior.
source: These results suggest that sensory or behavioral feedback from target animals can impact the operation of what may appear to be an 'execution mechanism' for a given behavior.
evidence: The claim is an inference drawn from the observed influence of target sex on behavior.

claim: The functional segregation of dsx and fru observed in this study can be considered analogous to the organizational and activation functions of sex hormones in mammals.
source: The functional segregation of dsx and fru that we observed can be considered analogous to the organizational and activation functions of sex hormones in mammals (McCarthy, 2008).
evidence: The claim is an inference based on comparison to known mechanisms in mammals, supported by a citation.

claim: dsx has an organizational function for the courtship execution circuit.
source: We postulate that dsx has an organizational function for the courtship execution circuit, whereas fru is important for the appropriate activation of the circuit.
evidence: The claim is a hypothesis based on the observed roles of dsx and fru in the study.

claim: fru is important for the appropriate activation of the courtship circuit.
source: We postulate that dsx has an organizational function for the courtship execution circuit, whereas fru is important for the appropriate activation of the circuit.
evidence: The claim is a hypothesis based on the observed roles of dsx and fru in the study.

claim: The wing extension execution circuit that connects NP2631 ∩ dsxFLP neurons and relevant motoneurons is specified even in the absence of fruM.
source: Nonetheless, our result suggests that the wing extension execution circuit that connects NP2631 ∩ dsxFLP neurons and relevant motoneurons is specified even in the absence of fruM (Pan et al., 2011), which is consistent with previous observations that fruF males are capable of expressing at least a part of courtship behavior (Demir and Dickson, 2005; Hall, 1978; Villella et al., 1997).
evidence: The claim is an inference drawn from the behavioral data in fruF males and is corroborated by citations to previous studies.

claim: dsx is important for the specification of a few other behaviorally relevant sexual dimorphisms in the Drosophila nervous system.
source: dsx is important for the specification of a few other behaviorally relevant sexual dimorphisms in the Drosophila nervous system.
evidence: The claim is supported by examples provided in the following sentences and citations.

claim: The sexually dimorphic axon development of leg gustatory receptor neurons requires dsx function.
source: For instance, the sexually dimorphic axon development of leg gustatory receptor neurons, which includes aphrodisiac pheromone sensors (Lu et al., 2012; Starostina et al., 2012; Thistle et al., 2012; Toda et al., 2012), requires dsx function (Mellert et al., 2010; Mellert et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The neural connectivity and function of TN1 neurons are specified by dsx.
source: The neural connectivity and function of TN1 neurons (Rideout et al., 2010; Robinett et al., 2010; Shirangi et al., 2016), which are pre-motor neurons important for the production of pulse song, are also specified by dsx (Shirangi et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Several classes of abdominal ganglia neurons involved in male copulation express dsx.
source: Several classes of abdominal ganglia neurons involved in male copulation also express dsx (Crickmore and Vosshall, 2013; Pavlou et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: dsx is involved in sex-determination across a variety of animal phyla.
source: It is noteworthy that dsx is involved in sex-determination across a variety of animal phyla (Kopp, 2012; Matson and Zarkower, 2012), whereas fru's role in sex-determination seems confined to insects (Gailey et al., 2006).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: fru's role in sex-determination seems confined to insects.
source: It is noteworthy that dsx is involved in sex-determination across a variety of animal phyla (Kopp, 2012; Matson and Zarkower, 2012), whereas fru's role in sex-determination seems confined to insects (Gailey et al., 2006).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: dsx may be evolutionarily more ancient in the context of sex-determination than fru, which can account for its dominance over fru when specifying sexually dimorphic neurons that co-express dsx and fru.
source: This suggests that dsx may be evolutionarily more ancient in the context of sex-determination than fru, which can account for its dominance over fru when specifying sexually dimorphic neurons that co-express dsx and fru.
evidence: The claim is a speculation based on the evolutionary distribution of dsx and fru.

claim: Many characterized fru-expressing neurons are involved in processing sex- and species-specific sensory cues.
source: Our proposal that fruM may be important for enhancing courtship behavior specifically towards females is consistent with the fact that many characterized fru-expressing neurons are involved in processing sex- and species-specific sensory cues (Clowney et al., 2015; Fan et al., 2013; Kallman et al., 2015; Kohl et al., 2013; Kurtovic et al., 2007; Lin et al., 2016; Lu et al., 2012; Ribeiro et al., 2018; Ruta et al., 2010; Starostina et al., 2012; Stockinger et al., 2005; Thistle et al., 2012; Toda et al., 2012; Yu et al., 2010; Zhou et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to multiple previous studies.

claim: P1a neurons, as well as more broadly defined P1/pC1 neurons, are known to respond to sex-specific chemical cues.
source: Namely, P1a neurons, as well as more broadly defined P1/pC1 neurons accessed by different genetic reagents, are known to respond to sex-specific chemical cues (Clowney et al., 2015; Kallman et al., 2015; Kohatsu et al., 2011), underscoring their critical role in sensory integration for courtship (Auer and Benton, 2016; Ellendersen and von Philipsborn, 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: fruM can play the 'activation' role for courtship by establishing sensory circuits that transmit sex-specific sensory information to P1/pC1 neurons.
source: fruM can play the 'activation' role for courtship by establishing sensory circuits that transmit sex-specific sensory information to P1/pC1 neurons (Ito et al., 2012; Ito et al., 2016; Kimura et al., 2005; von Philipsborn et al., 2014), or by enabling P1/pC1 neurons to properly integrate and transform such neural inputs.
evidence: The claim is a speculation about the mechanism, supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: fruM can play the 'activation' role for courtship by enabling P1/pC1 neurons to properly integrate and transform neural inputs.
source: fruM can play the 'activation' role for courtship by establishing sensory circuits that transmit sex-specific sensory information to P1/pC1 neurons (Ito et al., 2012; Ito et al., 2016; Kimura et al., 2005; von Philipsborn et al., 2014), or by enabling P1/pC1 neurons to properly integrate and transform such neural inputs.
evidence: The claim is a speculation about the mechanism.

claim: Neuroanatomical defects of P1a neurons in fruF males could disrupt either the establishment of sensory circuits or the integration of neural inputs.
source: Neuroanatomical defects of P1a neurons in fruF males could disrupt either process.
evidence: The claim is a speculation based on the observed neuroanatomical defects.

claim: A new class of fru-expressing neurons downstream of P1a neurons has been found to mediate the persistence of courtship behavior triggered by P1a neuronal activation.
source: Recently, a new class of fru-expressing neurons downstream of P1a neurons has been found to mediate the persistence of courtship behavior triggered by P1a neuronal activation (Jung et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to a recent study.

claim: fruM females can still perform wing extensions.
source: While we conclude that the role of fru is not necessarily to specify the execution mechanism for courtship behavior, fruM females can still perform wing extensions (Demir and Dickson, 2005; Rideout et al., 2007).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Artificial stimulation of either fru- or dsx-expressing neurons in females can elicit wing extensions.
source: Moreover, artificial stimulation of either fru- (Clyne and Miesenböck, 2008; Pan et al., 2011) or dsx- (Rezával et al., 2016) expressing neurons in females can elicit wing extensions, suggesting that the residual execution mechanism for at least a part of courtship behavior may be specified in a sex-invariant manner.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies and includes an inference about the mechanism.

claim: The presence of a latent mating execution circuit in female brains is also suggested in mice.
source: The presence of a latent mating execution circuit in female brains is also suggested in mice (Kimchi et al., 2007; Li and Dulac, 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies in mice.

claim: The courtship songs produced by females or fruM females are defective.
source: Because the courtship songs produced by females or fruM females are defective (Pan et al., 2011; Rezával et al., 2016; Rideout et al., 2007), male-type splicing of dsx nonetheless seems to be instrumental in organizing the proper execution mechanism for Drosophila courtship behavior.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies and includes an inference about the role of dsx.

claim: Male-type splicing of dsx seems to be instrumental in organizing the proper execution mechanism for Drosophila courtship behavior.
source: Because the courtship songs produced by females or fruM females are defective (Pan et al., 2011; Rezával et al., 2016; Rideout et al., 2007), male-type splicing of dsx nonetheless seems to be instrumental in organizing the proper execution mechanism for Drosophila courtship behavior.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the defective courtship songs in females and fruM females.

claim: At least one group of fruM-dependent neurons can promote male-type aggressive behaviors independent of dsx.
source: In Wohl et al. (2020), we found that at least one group of fruM-dependent neurons can promote male-type aggressive behaviors independent of dsx.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to a companion study.

claim: A separation of the courtship execution mechanism and the aggression execution mechanism by two sex-determining genes is likely accomplished by a partial separation of underlying neural circuits.
source: Therefore, a separation of the courtship execution mechanism and the aggression execution mechanism by two sex-determining genes is likely accomplished by a partial separation of underlying neural circuits.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the observed differential roles of dsx and fru in courtship and aggression.

claim: The aggression-promoting function of NP2631 ∩ dsxFLP and P1a neurons likely reflects their roles to coordinate aggression and courtship depending on internal and external conditions, instead of a simple decision switch that triggers fixed types of behavior.
source: The aggression-promoting function of NP2631 ∩ dsxFLP and P1a neurons likely reflects their roles to coordinate aggression and courtship depending on internal and external conditions, instead of a simple decision switch that triggers fixed types of behavior.
evidence: The claim is an inference about the function of these neurons based on the observed data.

claim: The sexually dimorphic morphology and wiring specificity of many fru-expressing neurons are determined in a cell-autonomous manner.
source: The sexually dimorphic morphology and wiring specificity of many fru-expressing neurons are determined in a cell-autonomous manner (Kimura et al., 2008; Kohl et al., 2013), suggesting that dsx and fru define Drosophila sex at a cellular level through regulation of a specific set of target genes (Dalton et al., 2013; Ito et al., 2012; Neville et al., 2014; Vernes, 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies and includes an inference about the mechanism.

claim: dsx and fru define Drosophila sex at a cellular level through regulation of a specific set of target genes.
source: The sexually dimorphic morphology and wiring specificity of many fru-expressing neurons are determined in a cell-autonomous manner (Kimura et al., 2008; Kohl et al., 2013), suggesting that dsx and fru define Drosophila sex at a cellular level through regulation of a specific set of target genes (Dalton et al., 2013; Ito et al., 2012; Neville et al., 2014; Vernes, 2015).
evidence: The claim is an inference supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Organismal sex can be regarded as a collective phenotype of genetic 'sexes' that can be reduced down to the cellular level.
source: Thus, both in flies and in mammals, organismal sex can be regarded as a collective phenotype of genetic 'sexes' that can be reduced down to the cellular level (Robinett et al., 2010; Williams and Carroll, 2009).
evidence: The claim is an inference supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: NP2631 ∩ dsxFLP and P1a neurons labeled by different genetic reagents are largely separate populations.
source: Surprisingly, we found that behaviorally relevant NP2631 ∩ dsxFLP and P1a neurons, as well as NP2631 ∩ fruFLP and P1a neurons, seldom overlap.
evidence: The claim is supported by neuroanatomical data presented in the study.

claim: Optogenetic stimulation of NP2631 ∩ dsxFLP and P1a neurons triggers social behaviors in temporally distinct manners.
source: Optogenetic stimulation of NP2631 ∩ dsxFLP and P1a neurons triggers social behaviors in temporally distinct manners.
evidence: The claim is supported by behavioral data presented in the study.

claim: fru has a different impact on the specification and function of NP2631 ∩ dsxFLP and P1a neurons.
source: Moreover, fru has a different impact on the specification and function of these two neuron groups, suggesting that little overlap of NP2631 ∩ dsxFLP and P1a neurons does not necessarily reflect arbitrary labeling bias within a single homogeneous neuronal population by different genetic reagents.
evidence: The claim is supported by neuroanatomical and behavioral data presented in the study.

claim: Little overlap of NP2631 ∩ dsxFLP and P1a neurons does not necessarily reflect arbitrary labeling bias within a single homogeneous neuronal population by different genetic reagents.
source: Moreover, fru has a different impact on the specification and function of these two neuron groups, suggesting that little overlap of NP2631 ∩ dsxFLP and P1a neurons does not necessarily reflect arbitrary labeling bias within a single homogeneous neuronal population by different genetic reagents.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the observed differences in specification and function.

claim: P1/pC1 neurons consist of functionally diverse subtypes.
source: Instead, these observations support the idea that of P1/pC1 neurons consist of functionally diverse subtypes.
evidence: The claim is a conclusion drawn from the observed diversity in neuroanatomy, behavior, and genetic specification.

claim: Differential expression patterns of FruM proteins within both NP2631 ∩ dsxFLP and P1a clusters suggest that heterogeneity almost certainly exists within these populations.
source: We acknowledge that the genetic reagents used in our study are likely insufficient to resolve the possible heterogeneity within either NP2631 ∩ dsxFLP or P1a neurons. Differential expression patterns of FruM proteins within both clusters (Figure 2—figure supplement 2C, Figure 5—figure supplement 1D) alone suggest that such heterogeneity almost certainly exists.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2C and Figure 5—figure supplement 1D.
